This system is shown to be equivalent to the clause collection tree calculus, and it is capable of simulating the resolution calculus. A proof system called sequent calculus with the cut rule is also introduced, and it is shown to be equivalent to the clause collection cycles calculus. This calculus is capable of simulating the resolution calculus. A new proof method called induction is introduced, which is a generalization of the clause collection cycles calculus. This method is capable of proving a given sequent by induction on the length of the given proof. A new proof method called clause collection cycles is also introduced, which is a generalization of the clause collection trees. This method is capable of proving a given sequent by induction on the length of the given proof.

This study introduces a novel graph retrieval model, ALIGN, which leverages a
knowledge graph to retrieve relevant subgraphs for a given query. ALIGN is trained
using a contrastive learning approach, where a retrieval model and an aligner are
employed to create a shared embedding space. Our model's performance is evaluated
on the KGIN benchmark, where it surpasses the current state-of-the-art by a
substantial margin, achieving a 10% increase in MAP score. Additionally, we
conduct an ablation study to assess the impact of various components in our model.
The source code for our research is available at https://github.com/leewei-ntu/ALIGN.

This research introduces a novel approach to enhancing the performance of neural networks in transient dynamics modeling by drawing inspiration from natural language processing techniques. The proposed method leverages a language model to forecast the subsequent states of a system, given its current state, and evaluates its efficacy on two distinct power systems. The study reveals that integrating the language model into the training process yields a substantial improvement in both accuracy and training speed.

In the context of large-scale electricity distribution, we examine how to fairly allocate electricity to a group of users, each with a unique demand and billing system. The challenge lies in determining the amount of electricity each user receives, given the provider's total available electricity and revenue target. We propose a framework for analyzing these allocations, which allows us to establish a key result: a finite number of distinct scenarios exist for allocating a given amount of electricity, and these scenarios can be efficiently calculated. This framework is used to develop a linear division algorithm, which can be modified to meet specific fairness criteria. We also explore the potential of using this approach to create a fair electricity distribution system that takes into account the specific needs of each user.

The task of event coreference resolution has been extensively researched in domains such as biology and sports, but this study focuses on a more complex area: identifying coreferential events in controversial politics news reports. To this end, we have compiled the WE-CORE, a dataset consisting of over 1,000 annotated sentences from news reports covering 26 significant political events. To evaluate the effectiveness of current methods, we have tested both rule-based and neural network approaches on this dataset, and our results indicate that neural networks outperform existing rule-based methods. Furthermore, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the challenges associated with event coreference resolution in news reports and the impact of these difficulties on the performance of the WE-CORE dataset.

The complementarity knapsack problem is a variant of the knapsack problem, where variables are either 0 or 1, and their relationship is defined by a complementarity constraint. This constraint requires that if two variables are both 1, then their product must be 0. The integer linear programming relaxation of the problem is used to solve it, and its facets are crucial in understanding the problem's behavior. This paper introduces a new method for identifying facets in the problem's relaxation, and it provides a way to verify the significance of these facets. The method relies on a new class of sets that are crucial in understanding the problem's behavior, and it is shown that facets in the problem's relaxation can be found using these sets. The paper also provides a new method for identifying facets in the problem's relaxation, and it provides a new understanding of the problem's behavior.
This paper establishes the existence of certain types of centralizers and derivations within specific, non-factorizable algebras.

A long-standing issue in particle physics is the origin of chiral symmetry breaking, which is crucial for understanding the mass of fermions. In his groundbreaking work, Weinberg proposed a distinct mechanism for this phenomenon, which relies on a two-factor relationship between the chiral symmetry breaking and the scale of the theory. In this study, we demonstrate that this two-factor relationship is a direct outcome of the fundamental spin constraints inherent in the theory.

We establish that for any given dimension n, there exists a threshold K such that for any K-exponential map from n to n-1 dimensions, the integral of the inverse of the measure of the transversal set is at least one. This result has implications for two specific cases. Firstly, it addresses a question posed by Orponen and Vuorinen about the relationship between the measure of the transversal set of an n-dimensional curve and n-dimensional space, and secondly, it provides a generalization of Favavre's theorem to nonlinear projections.

This research paper presents a novel approach to reinforcement learning that incorporates a directed search method, specifically tube model predictive control, to address the issue of demonstration efficiency. The proposed method, DR-Tube MPC, is capable of learning policies that are robust to uncertainties in a single shot, without relying on any specific distribution of expert demonstrations. The proposed method is demonstrated to be effective in a challenging scenario, where a quadrotor is tasked with navigating through a narrow passage while avoiding obstacles, and is shown to be more efficient than existing methods in terms of the number of demonstrations required.

A theoretical model for the intrinsic unusual Hall effect has been developed, which is based on a mathematical framework that incorporates band structure and is applicable to both two and three-dimensional systems. This framework reveals that the Hall conductivity can be broken down into two distinct components: one related to the geometry of the electronic bands and another connected to the electronic scattering processes. This decomposition enables the separation of the intrinsic Hall conductivity from the extrinsic contributions, which arise from the electronic scattering. This theoretical model has been successfully applied to a specific material, MoTe2, to calculate the electronic scattering-induced Hall conductivity. This material exhibits a significant scattering-induced Hall effect, which is attributed to the presence of a Berry curvature dipole.

To assess the effectiveness of software testing techniques, researchers need to compare the behavior of different testing approaches.  To achieve this, they rely on call graph representations of the code that was tested, which are then compared to measure the effectiveness of each testing technique.  However, comparing these call graphs is a complex task, requiring the use of a specific type of algorithm known as graph edit distance.  Unfortunately, this type of algorithm is computationally expensive and impractical for large-scale comparisons.  To address this issue, we have developed a novel method that uses a more efficient representation of call graphs to enable faster comparisons.  Our approach involves a new algorithm that can compare large collections of call graphs in a scalable manner, and we have demonstrated its effectiveness through a series of experiments.

The "one billion word benchmark" has been used to compare the performance of MT systems by testing them on a limited dataset with varying amounts of information. This study examines the assumption that more information leads to better results by analyzing the different versions of the benchmark. It found that the amount of information provided in the benchmark actually increases, rather than decreases, with added context, which contradicts the idea that the benchmark is a reliable measure of progress. This suggests that the benchmark may not accurately reflect real-world MT performance and that researchers should be cautious when interpreting results from it.

A key phenomenon in solar flares, known as a flare current sheet, is believed to be the primary driver of particle acceleration. However, the exact nature of this structure remains unclear due to the lack of high-resolution observations. A recent study of a solar flare observed by the RHESSI telescope revealed that the quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) in the hard X-ray emissions are caused by the microwave emissions from the flare current sheet. By analyzing the RHESSI data, the researchers found that the QPOs in the microwave emissions have a consistent frequency of 0.12 Hz, which is significantly higher than the frequency of the QPOs in the hard X-ray emissions. This finding suggests that the flare current sheet is responsible for the microwave emissions. Furthermore, the researchers found that the microwave emissions are modulated by the same frequency as the QPOs in the hard X-ray emissions, which is consistent with the hypothesis that the flare current sheet is responsible for the microwave emissions. This study provides new insights into the structure and dynamics of the flare current sheet, and may help to improve our understanding of solar flares.

In industrial anomaly detection, the goal is to identify deviations from the standard, or "normal" class, in a dataset. However, the "normal" class in industrial settings is often characterized by a diverse range of variations, making it difficult to define a clear boundary. To address this challenge, we propose a novel, multi-scale approach that utilizes a statistical model to identify anomalies. This method, grounded in the "contrario" principle, is designed to be robust against variations in lighting, object orientation, and other factors. By employing a Gaussian Mixture Model, our approach can effectively capture the complexity of the "normal" class and detect anomalies in a wide range of applications. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method, particularly in scenarios where the "normal" class is highly variable.

This study examines the local well-posedness of a modified Kadomtsev--Petviashvili equation, specifically focusing on a dispersion-generalized model. The research proves the equation's local well-posedness for initial data in certain Besov spaces under the condition that the sum of the data's spatial dimensions is less than one plus half the equation's parameter. The study also extends previous results on well-posedness, broadening the range of applicable parameters and data spaces.

In quantum systems with specific symmetries, certain states can share identical energy levels, but when these symmetries are disrupted, these shared energy levels can split. We investigate how the symmetry in quantum systems with unique properties is affected by their interaction with the environment. We discovered that when quantum systems with specific properties interact with their surroundings, the symmetry can be disrupted, leading to a splitting of the shared energy levels. We also found that this splitting can be restored through a process involving the exchange of information between the system and its surroundings. Our findings have implications for the development of quantum technologies, as they show that the symmetry can be affected by the type of interaction between the system and its surroundings.

In wireless networks, accurately predicting future channel state information (CSI) is crucial for optimizing performance. This paper introduces a novel, low-complexity method for forecasting the CSI response of highly-mobile users in massive MIMO systems. By modeling the user's movement as a random walk, the approach uses a first-order autoregressive model to forecast CSI based on historical data. This method is applied to a massive MIMO system, and its effectiveness is evaluated through simulations, demonstrating that it outperforms existing methods in terms of spectral efficiency.

This paper proposes a novel approach to measure the degree of overlap between two distinct distributions, specifically, the probability that one distribution's values are less than a specified threshold. This probability, known as the minor region, is a key metric in determining the similarity between two populations. To estimate the minor region, the paper presents a method that utilizes a combination of beta distributions, which are suitable for modeling a wide range of probabilities. This method is effective in handling complex distributions, including those with multiple modes, and is capable of handling datasets with various types of data. The proposed approach is supported by theoretical results and is further validated through numerical examples and applications to real-world datasets.

We establish an asymptotic expansion for the Szeg\H{o} projector's kernel on the boundary of the complexification of a compact, strictly pseudoconvex manifold. This expansion is derived from an asymptotic scaling of the kernel on a specific region of Grauert's tube.

The Reverse Line Chart technique, first introduced by Roussopoulos in 2000, has been a significant breakthrough in data visualization. However, a new algorithm, known as MARINLINGA, has been developed to create Reverse Line Charts, which boasts several key advantages over the original method. MARINLINGA boasts a more efficient time complexity of O(n^2), compared to Roussopoulos's method of O(n^3), and offers a more user-friendly interface. Furthermore, it can handle a broader range of data, including negative values. To demonstrate its effectiveness, MARINLINGA has been applied to a real-world case study, showcasing its potential for practical use.

This paper serves as a practical application of a theoretical framework from [1], which outlines an approach to analyzing the topological structure of rigid modules. We provide concrete examples that validate the key findings of the framework, specifically in the context of a particular type of non-archimedean function field geometry.

Java's dependency system has become a cornerstone of the language, enabling developers to easily integrate third-party libraries into their applications. However, certain dependencies, known as "inflated dependencies," are particularly problematic due to their excessive size, which can significantly impact the performance of Java applications. This study focuses on Java's Maven Central repository, a central hub for open-source software, to investigate the prevalence and characteristics of inflated dependencies. By analyzing a comprehensive dataset of Maven Central's contents, we discovered that inflated dependencies are relatively rare, comprising only 1.5% of the total dependencies. Furthermore, we found that inflated dependencies are predominantly large, with a median size of 12.5 MB, and are often used in popular packages. Our analysis also revealed that inflated dependencies are more likely to be used in production environments, particularly in web applications, and are often employed in specific contexts, such as data processing and network communication. This study provides valuable insights into the behavior of inflated dependencies and can help developers and researchers better understand the Java ecosystem.

The study of complex biological systems has been a long-standing pursuit in biology, but recent breakthroughs in synthetic biology have enabled the creation of artificial systems that can self-replicate and evolve. Our research focuses on a new method for creating artificial life forms using the principles of synthetic biology. By using a technique called biphoton regulated synthesis, we have successfully created artificial systems that can replicate and evolve, and our results show that these systems can be used to study the behavior of complex systems. Our findings suggest that these artificial systems can be used to test new ideas and theories about how complex systems work, and they may also have potential applications in the development of new technologies and systems.

In a complex, multi-stage decision-making process, a decision-maker faces uncertainty in each stage, requiring them to make informed choices based on current and anticipated scenarios. To address this challenge, a two-part strategy is employed: first, a scenario selection method identifies a set of likely outcomes with minimal risk, and second, a multi-stage optimization problem is formulated to maximize performance under various scenarios. To tackle scenario selection, a novel approach is proposed, which leverages the concept of distributional resilience to minimize the difference between the actual and selected scenario distributions. By using total variation discrepancy, a new formulation is developed to find a set of scenarios with the smallest possible discrepancy, and this approach is further refined to incorporate a scenario selection method that considers the decision-maker's perspective. The approach is demonstrated through a numerical case study on a multistage facility location problem, showcasing its effectiveness in identifying efficient scenarios.

This paper proposes a novel approach to action prediction using a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) enhanced by Radial Basis Function (RBF) kernel-based feature mapping. The proposed method, known as RBF-RNN, overcomes the limitations of traditional RNNs by incorporating a mapping layer that utilizes the RBF kernel to capture complex relationships between input features. The RBF-RNN architecture is composed of two main components: a mapping layer that projects input features into a higher-dimensional space and a recurrent layer that processes the projected features. The proposed method is evaluated on the NTU-RGB+D dataset and achieves superior performance compared to state-of-the-art methods, demonstrating its effectiveness in action prediction tasks.

Deep learning's ability to model complex systems has been demonstrated, yet its application to systems in thermal equilibrium remains limited. A novel approach to this challenge is presented, which utilizes unique time scales to optimize the performance of deep learning models. This method is applied to a complex spin system, and its effectiveness is shown to be superior to traditional models, particularly in cases where the system's complexity is high. A key aspect of this approach is the use of specialized activation functions, which enable the system to accurately capture the system's behavior over time. A mathematical framework is developed to analyze the system's performance, and its ability to generalize to new situations is demonstrated. This approach has the potential to be applied to a wide range of complex systems, and its ability to provide accurate predictions in cases where the system's behavior is difficult to understand.

This study delves into the properties of boundedness and nuclearity of a class of pseudo-differential operators on a uniform tree that excludes any branches with a degree of two. The research utilizes a symbolic approach to analyze these operators. The framework developed here is based on a specific transform, which is analogous to the Fourier transform, known as the spectral transform. The study also establishes the conditions under which pseudo-differential operators with symbols belonging to specific symbol classes are bounded on a space of functions. Additionally, it is shown that pseudo-differential operators with symbols belonging to another symbol class are nuclear.

This research paper delves into the characteristics of the Visibility Domain (VD) in 5G networks, a key area of study that has gained significant attention in the context of IoT networks. The VD is defined as the set of devices that a given device can detect within its communication range. The authors introduce the concept of VD-based applications, which leverage the VD to gather data and perform various tasks. The authors then present a comprehensive analysis of VD-based applications, highlighting their potential and limitations. The authors also present a case study that demonstrates the VD's potential in a real-world scenario, where it is used to monitor the health of a 5G network. The authors conclude by discussing the VD's limitations and suggesting future research directions.

Deep neural networks often display a tendency to overestimate their performance, particularly when encountering data that falls outside their training set. This phenomenon is particularly concerning in safety-critical applications, where the reliability of these models is paramount. To address this issue, we introduce Code, a novel method that generates new data points that are not part of the training set. Our approach is grounded in the observation that the likelihood of a data point being part of the training set can be accurately estimated using the Chamfer distance. Our experiments demonstrate that the generated data points are indeed out-of-distribution, and that outperform existing methods in capturing the uncertainty of a model when encountering new data.

The 2-jet, 3-jet, and 4-jet inclusive events in pp collisions at 13 TeV are studied using the 2015-2016 LHCb data. The analysis focuses on the azimuthal relationships between the jets, particularly the angle between the leading and subleading jets, as well as the angles between the leading and subleading jets and the third leading jet. The findings are compared to the predictions of the parton shower model Pythia 8, which includes the matrix element corrections.

Deep learning has become a prominent approach in computer vision, particularly in tasks like image classification, object detection, and segmentation. However, the effectiveness of deep learning models heavily relies on the availability of large-scale, high-quality datasets, which is often a limitation in real-world applications. To address this challenge, researchers have developed various semi-supervised and unsupervised learning techniques that can leverage limited labeled data or no labeled data at all. This survey provides a comprehensive overview of the current state-of-the-art in semi-supervised and unsupervised deep learning for computer vision, focusing on the challenges, methodologies, and applications in this field.

Identifying unusual data points in a dataset is a critical task in machine learning, particularly when dealing with anomaly detection. This process is crucial for detecting malicious activities, such as fraud or cyber attacks, in real-world applications. This study focuses on comparing the effectiveness of different reconstruction error metrics used in outlier detection. We examine the performance of three commonly employed reconstruction error metrics, namely $L_1$, $L_2$, and $L_{\infty}$ norms, in the context of two prominent unsupervised learning techniques: autoencoders and variational autoencoders. We assess the accuracy of these methods in detecting outliers on a diverse set of datasets, including both numerical and categorical data. Our findings suggest that the $L_1$ norm outperforms the other metrics in terms of accuracy, particularly on datasets containing categorical data.

This study delves into the nuances of pathwise solutions for nonlinear Young equations, focusing on the nuances of nonlinear functional equations. We derive a novel result demonstrating the uniqueness of locally Hölder continuous functions that satisfy these equations, provided the functions adhere to certain conditions. We further establish the existence of such functions under appropriate hypotheses. We apply our findings to derive new results for both random and deterministic rough differential equations, and we extend the theory to non-Lipschitz stochastic PDEs with rough boundaries, providing new insights into the existence and uniqueness of strong solutions.

A straightforward approach to measure neutrino structure is through their interactions with external magnetic and electric fields, which can be described by the polarizability of neutrinos. In this study, we have calculated the polarizability of neutrinos in a vacuum and in matter, and our results are compared to the existing theoretical predictions.

The interplay between neurons and glial cells plays a significant role in the brain's complex electrical activity. To study this interaction, researchers have developed a model that incorporates the cells' electrical properties and their connections. This model reveals that the system can exhibit various behaviors, including oscillations and chaos, depending on the strength of the connections between the cells. By examining the system's patterns, researchers have identified a specific type of oscillation that occurs when the cells are connected strongly. This type of oscillation is characterized by a specific pattern of activity, where the cells are either highly active or completely silent. By analyzing the system's patterns, researchers have developed a method to create rhythmic patterns of activity, which can be used to understand the brain's complex electrical activity.

The study of a neutral particle with spin-1/2 in a magnetic field reveals novel topological properties. The particle's motion is influenced by an external magnetic field, which can be mathematically represented as a gauge field. The particle's spin is treated as a vector field, which is then quantized to yield a Hamiltonian with both bosonic and fermionic components. The Hamiltonian's eigenvalues and eigenstates are calculated, and the resulting wave functions are found to exhibit topological properties. The study shows that the wave functions can be either Abelian or non-Abelian, depending on the particle's energy levels. The non-Abelian wave functions are found to be particularly interesting, as they exhibit a unique topological structure. The study also investigates the behavior of the non-Abelian wave functions under various gauge transformations, and the resulting topological properties are found to be robust against such transformations. The study's findings suggest that the non-Abelian wave functions could be used to develop new types of topological quantum computing schemes.

The phenomenon of boundary erosion in diffusion processes is characterized by a gradual thinning of the diffusion layer, which occurs when particles pass through a boundary and then diffuse back into the original space. This process is distinct from traditional diffusion with absorbing boundaries, where particles that pass through a boundary are removed from the system. In this study, we investigate the diffusion process with particles that pass through a boundary and then diffuse back into the original space, where the boundary thins over time. We derive the mean first passage time (MFPT) for this process and show that it exhibits a power-law behavior, which is different from the traditional case. We also derive the asymptotic behavior of the MFPT for this process and show that it is given by a power-law function of the diffusion coefficient. This result is in contrast to the traditional case, where the MFPT diverges as the diffusion coefficient approaches zero. We also derive the asymptotic behavior of the distribution of the first passage time for this process and show that it is given by a power-law function of the diffusion coefficient. This result is in contrast to the traditional case, where the distribution of the first passage time is exponential. We also discuss the implications of these results for the understanding of the boundary erosion phenomenon.

A link is classified as an $n$-l-space link if its $n$-component sublinks are all identified as l-space links. This paper focuses on a subset of l-space links with hyperbolic components and develops the notion of a formal semigroup tied to these links. The primary finding is that l-space links linked with a specific class of torus links are not classified as $n$-l-space links for any value of $n$. The study also includes a comprehensive analysis of the links linked with the torus links $T(2,5)$, $T(2,6)$, and $T(3,3)$, presenting specific information about their boundary slopes and the number of simple closed geodesics on their complements' complete hyperbolic surfaces.

A generalized kinetic theory for a gas in a non-constant random environment is formulated, and the corresponding Poisson bracket is derived. This theory is then used to develop the hydrodynamic equations for a non-constant disorder medium, and the relationship between the two is established.

The use of computer vision in endoscopic videos has the potential to significantly improve patient safety by identifying artifacts and foreign objects. However, existing research has primarily focused on single object detectors, neglecting the need for comprehensive evaluation of object detection systems. To address this gap, we propose a new evaluation framework that assesses the performance of object detectors in endoscopic settings. We also introduce novel metrics to measure the accuracy of object detection systems in terms of their bounding box accuracy and the accuracy of their predicted categories. Our proposed framework is applied to a new dataset, called the Endoscopic Object Detection Challenge 2021 dataset, which contains 1,000 annotated endoscopic images. We evaluate 12 leading object detection systems using our framework and demonstrate that a combination of these systems can effectively identify artifacts in endoscopic videos. Our results show that the proposed framework can be used to improve the reliability of object detection systems in medical settings.

This research delves into the underlying principles of syntax patterns in source code identifiers, focusing on their formation and meaning. Through an in-depth examination of syntax patterns, we discovered that they are primarily composed of two to three components, with the majority consisting of only two. We also found that these patterns are predominantly formed through concatenation, with a significant portion of them being of English origin. Moreover, our analysis revealed that these patterns are not only used for identification but also convey specific information about the classes they represent. By examining the patterns' meanings, we found that they are often used to describe the classes' functionality, with a significant portion of them being used to indicate the classes' purpose or function. We also found that these patterns are not randomly generated, but rather created by developers with a specific purpose in mind. Our findings suggest that these patterns are not only used for identification but also serve as a means of communication between developers.

This article presents a novel approach to constructing the $\square_q$-structure on the Fock space of the quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, by leveraging the $q$-shuffle algebra framework. The $\square_q$-structure is a crucial component in the study of the quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$, as it is a fundamental building block for the quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ and the quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$ with a specific type of symmetry. The construction of the $\square_q$-structure is based on a novel idea of using the $q$-shuffle algebra framework to derive the $\square_q$-structure. The article also provides a detailed analysis of the $\square_q$-structure and its implications for the quantum affine $\mathfrak{sl}_2$.

The study of grain growth in polycrystalline materials is a fundamental aspect of materials science, with a long history of research. However, the complexity of grain growth in multi-phase systems, such as duplex and triplex systems, poses significant challenges due to the interplay of different phases. This research focuses on grain growth in two- and three-phase systems, with a particular emphasis on the effects of different phase compositions and grain boundary properties. By employing a data-driven approach, the study investigates the grain growth kinetics in various microstructures, with a focus on understanding the underlying mechanisms. The results reveal that grain growth kinetics can be accurately described by a simple power-law model, with a notable dependence on the volume fraction of different phases. The study also highlights the importance of grain boundary properties in determining the grain growth behavior, with a particular emphasis on the effects of grain boundary mobility and misorientation. Overall, the research provides valuable insights into the grain growth process in multi-phase systems, with potential implications for the design of materials with tailored microstructures and properties.

Significant advancements have been made in the field of 3D human pose and shape estimation, particularly in the context of single-person pose estimation. However, the majority of research has focused on the development of algorithms, with limited attention paid to the underlying data and its impact on the performance of these models. This study aims to bridge this gap by investigating the effect of data on the accuracy of 3D human pose and shape estimation. To achieve this, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of 3D human pose and shape estimation benchmarks, which includes 23 datasets from 14 sources. We have thoroughly analyzed the characteristics of these datasets and the results of 3D human pose and shape estimation methods, with a focus on the influence of data on the accuracy of these models. Our analysis reveals that the size of the dataset and the diversity of the data are key factors in determining the accuracy of 3D human pose and shape estimation methods. Furthermore, we have found that the data used in 3D human pose and shape estimation methods can be improved by incorporating more diverse and varied datasets. Our study provides valuable insights into the field of 3D human pose and shape estimation and highlights the importance of data in the development of accurate models.

A simplified model of a superconductor consisting of isolated sites with minimal electron interaction is proposed, where the sites are arranged in a grid and electrons interact with each other in a repulsive manner. The model reveals that a unique type of superconductivity emerges when the sites are relatively close to one another, characterized by a distinct pairing mechanism involving electrons of the same site. The model's behavior is analyzed using a combination of numerical and analytical methods, and the results show that the superconductivity is robust and can be controlled by adjusting the sites' spacing. The model's predictions are in good agreement with numerical simulations and provide insights into the nature of the superconducting state.

We've developed a matching framework for scalar leptoquarks, which is compatible with all possible interactions and operator basis, and is applicable to both SMEFT and EFT frameworks. Our work involves calculating one-loop corrections to operator coefficients, which are then used to determine the leptoquark parameters.

This paper examines the performance of machine learning classification in comparison to traditional statistical classification methods. We highlight the differences between these two approaches, specifically focusing on the unique aspects of machine learning that enable it to excel in certain areas. We then provide an overview of the fundamental concepts of statistical classification, including the Bayes classifier and the Naive Bayes classifier, before delving into the principles of machine learning classification. We explore key concepts such as the bias-variance trade-off, overfitting, and underfitting, and discuss the role of the training set in machine learning. We also examine the evaluation of machine learning algorithms, including the use of cross-validation and the comparison of different performance metrics. We discuss the challenges of evaluating machine learning algorithms, particularly in the context of high-dimensional data, and explore the use of feature selection and dimensionality reduction techniques. We also examine the use of regularization and the comparison of different performance metrics, such as the F1 score and the ROC curve. We conclude by discussing the future directions of machine learning research, including the use of deep learning and the integration of machine learning with other fields such as physics and biology.

This study introduces a control strategy for second-order systems that can be represented by a specific model. It utilizes a sliding-mode control approach to ensure system stability and robustness, even in the presence of unknown disturbances. A key innovation lies in the use of a simplified switching function, which allows for a more efficient and precise control of the system's state. Furthermore, the research provides a detailed analysis of the control's performance, including an estimate of the time required for the system to converge to the desired state.

The internal structure of lithium-ion batteries is complex and constantly changing, which makes it difficult to study using traditional methods. To address this, researchers have developed a new technique that uses ultrasonic vibrations to analyze the internal structure of lithium-ion batteries. By measuring how these vibrations change over time, researchers can gain insights into the internal layers of the battery. This study shows that this technique can be used to study how the internal layers of the battery change during charging and discharging, and that it can be used to identify the internal layers of the battery. This research has implications for developing new methods for monitoring and maintaining lithium-ion batteries.

This paper presents a novel flatness-oriented control approach for gantry cranes, 
utilizing trajectory planning to circumvent excitable dynamics. The proposed method 
is based on an innovative discrete-time model of the gantry crane, 
enabling the use of flatness for precise trajectory planning. The approach 
guarantees convergence to the desired target position, while also ensuring 
constraint satisfaction through a recursive feasibility condition. The feasibility 
of the proposed method is demonstrated through numerical simulations.

The majority of current research on image-to-text models heavily relies on clean data, but in real-world scenarios, images often contain noise, such as incorrect descriptions. This paper introduces a novel cooperative distillation approach to address the issue of noisy data in image description tasks. By leveraging the complementary strengths of image-to-text and text-to-image models, our method effectively minimizes the negative impact of noisy data on image descriptions. Experimental results on two large-scale datasets demonstrate the superior performance of our method in comparison to existing approaches.

We examine sets of sequences in a metric space that adhere to a specific connectivity metric, and demonstrate the existence of such sets that possess cardinality equal to the continuum. This leads to several applications, including a refinement of an existing result regarding unbounded connectivity in Banach spaces, and the identification of a class of metric spaces that feature bounded, highly-connected sets of cardinality equal to the continuum.

This paper delves into the concept of arranged homomorphisms between Ehresmann semigroups, focusing on arranged and completely embedded homomorphisms. It establishes a fundamental theorem that characterizes Ehresmann semigroups through their arranged homomorphisms. Additionally, a similar outcome is demonstrated for categories.

The self-attention mechanism in Transformer models is a crucial component that has garnered significant interest in recent years. Researchers have proposed various attention variants to improve efficiency, but surprisingly, the impact of increasing the model's depth on its performance has not been thoroughly examined. This study investigates the effect of increasing the depth of self-attention models on their performance, specifically focusing on the impact of depth and width on self-attention. The results show that increasing the depth of self-attention models leads to improved performance, but this benefit diminishes as the model's width decreases. The study also reveals that the benefits of depth are more pronounced in more complex tasks, suggesting that deeper self-attention models are particularly effective in handling intricate tasks. The findings of this study provide valuable insights into the design of self-attention models and can guide future research in this area.

We have synthesized BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles at a reduced temperature of 500°C, which resulted in a significant increase in their magnetic properties. The nanoparticles were characterized by a reduced grain size and a higher degree of crystallinity, as evidenced by X-ray diffraction analysis. The nanoparticles also exhibited a higher saturation magnetization of 10.5 emu/g, which is significantly higher than the bulk material. The nanoparticles were found to possess a higher photocatalytic activity in the degradation of Rhodamine B dye, with a rate constant of 0.0015 min$^{-1}$, which is significantly higher than that of the bulk material. The nanoparticles were also found to be effective in the production of hydrogen gas from water, with a rate of 0.0015 mL/min, which is significantly higher than that of the bulk material. The enhanced magnetic properties and photocatalytic activity of the nanoparticles are attributed to the reduced grain size and the presence of defects in the crystal structure. The results of this study suggest that the synthesis of BiFeO$_{3}$ nanoparticles at a reduced temperature is a promising approach to enhance the magnetic and photocatalytic properties of the material.

In a simplified model, we investigate the masses of the bottom quark and the tau lepton, which are both third generation particles. By examining the symmetry breaking pattern, we find that the masses of these particles are influenced by a unique combination of Yukawa couplings and symmetry breaking parameters. The model's predictions for the masses of these particles are in good agreement with experimental data, particularly for the masses of the bottom quark and the tau lepton. The model's predictions for the masses of the top quark and the other particles are also in line with experimental data.

Reconstructing three-dimensional images of unfamiliar objects held in the hand is a complex task, primarily due to the significant impact of hand poses on the resulting object shapes. To address this challenge, we've developed a new method that utilizes a single image to accurately reconstruct three-dimensional images of objects in their entirety. Our approach involves a novel two-stage process: first, we use a hand pose estimation network to determine the hand's position and orientation; then, we use this information to refine the object's 3D model through a multi-view image generation process. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on two datasets, showcasing its ability to produce high-quality 3D images of objects in various scenarios.

The Ca II and H-alpha spectral lines are widely used as reliable indicators of solar activity due to their high visibility in the solar atmosphere. These lines are particularly useful for studying the solar chromosphere, as they are strongly influenced by magnetic fields. The Ca-K and H-alpha lines are also used to identify solar active regions and coronal mass ejections. In this study, we have analyzed the Ca-K and H-alpha images from the Kodaikanal Observatory over a century-long period, and found that the Ca-K and H-alpha activity indices are highly correlated. We have also discovered that the Ca-K and H-alpha activity indices are strongly correlated with the sunspot number, and that the Ca-K and H-alpha activity indices are more closely related to the sunspot number than to the Ca-K and H-alpha activity indices. In addition, we have found that the Ca-K and H-alpha activity indices are more closely related to the sunspot number than to the Ca-K and H-alpha activity indices. In conclusion, our study has shown that the Ca-K and H-alpha activity indices are more closely related to the sunspot number than to the Ca-K and H-alpha activity indices.

The LHCb experiment has recently reported a measurement of the branching fraction for the Sigma plus to proton muon pair decay, which is the first of its kind. This measurement is in line with theoretical predictions and the previously measured decay rate for the Sigma plus to proton photon decay. This result is significant as it confirms the presence of this decay mode and provides valuable insights into the properties of the Sigma plus particle.

In distributed systems, assessing the impact of changes is crucial for maintaining stability, but it's challenging to do so due to the complexity of distributed programs. Existing methods often fail to accurately identify the scope of faults in distributed systems, leading to unnecessary system-wide outages. To address this limitation, a new approach has been developed that uses a depth-based metric to assess the impact of changes in distributed systems. This approach, called Distributed Symbolic Assessment, utilizes a unique metric to identify the scope of faults in distributed systems, which is then used to isolate and resolve issues without disrupting the entire system. This approach has been shown to be effective in a variety of distributed systems, including those with complex topologies and high levels of concurrency.

We investigate the aging process in a group of interacting superparamagnetic nanoparticles, which exhibit a phase transition between ordered and disordered states. The energy barrier for the system increases as the system ages, but this trend is disrupted when the nanoparticles are subjected to an external magnetic field, resulting in a rejuvenation effect. The group of nanoparticles is found to behave like a single, larger nanoparticle, but the energy barrier for the group is significantly higher than that of an individual nanoparticle, resulting in slower aging. The group's behavior is also influenced by the temperature at which the group is subjected to, resulting in a rejuvenation effect that is more pronounced at lower temperatures.

Federated learning allows for training models on decentralized networks without the need for a central server, which is particularly beneficial for social networks where users want to maintain data privacy.  However, traditional federated learning relies on a central server, which poses security risks in social networks where users may not trust each other.  To address this issue, we propose a new approach called SHIELD, which enables secure training of models on social networks without requiring a central server.  Our method leverages the trust relationships between users to create a framework that ensures model training security.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through experiments on real-world social networks, which show that SHIELD can achieve comparable model performance to traditional federated learning while maintaining security in decentralized settings.

The Short Text Categorization (STC) task is a complex challenge in Natural Language Processing (NLP) due to its inherent difficulties. This study introduces a novel approach to address the issue by leveraging the sequential nature of STC data. By incorporating both recurrent and convolutional neural network architectures, our model effectively captures the sequential dependencies in STC data. The proposed model is evaluated on four benchmark STC datasets, and the experimental results demonstrate its superiority over existing state-of-the-art methods.

The paper provides a comprehensive analytical description of telecentric Fabry-Perot etalons, which are characterized by parallel mirrors perpendicular to the incident light beam. This setup is particularly useful for applications such as spectrometers and filters. By examining the spectral response of telecentric resonators, the authors derive an analytical expression for the FWHM of the transmission peaks, which is in agreement with numerical simulations.

This study examines the properties of two types of pairings, which are established between the moduli space of stable parabolic log maps and certain moduli spaces of objects within parabolic sheaves. Specifically, we investigate the pairing, which was initially introduced by the authors in a previous work, and its counterpart, which is related to the moduli space of parabolic bundles and their modifications. Our analysis reveals that the first pairing is unimodular, and we also establish the conditions under which the second pairing is non-degenerate.

This technique has the potential to significantly speed up complex computations by utilizing specialized processing units. To facilitate this, we have developed an innovative framework that enables chiplets to work together seamlessly. This enables chiplets to be easily combined to create diverse computing systems, from basic processors to advanced systems with multiple processing units. In semiparametric mixture cure models, a subject's survival status is divided into two groups: those who have already recovered from the disease and those who are still at risk. The recovery probability is modeled using parametric methods, while the distribution of remaining failure times is described using parametric or nonparametric approaches. This study focuses on a specific type of mixture cure model, where the recovery probability is described using a logistic function and the distribution of remaining failure times is modeled using an unspecified nonparametric function. A new estimation method, based on a combination of local linear regression and maximum likelihood, is proposed to estimate the parameters of this model. The proposed estimator is shown to have desirable statistical properties, including consistency and asymptotic normality. The performance of this estimator is evaluated through a simulation study, and a real-world data analysis is presented to illustrate its practical utility.

In-memory processing (IMP) offers a promising solution to overcome the limitations of traditional computing systems, but it also presents new security concerns. The integration of processing capabilities into memory significantly reduces data exposure, yet it also makes the memory itself a more attractive target for attackers. The unique security vulnerabilities of IMPs, including those related to side-channel attacks, are not well understood. This study aims to investigate the security implications of IMPs, specifically the X86-based Myx16 architecture, and to identify vulnerabilities that could be exploited by side-channel attacks. The research highlights the importance of side-channel security in IMPs, as it can be a significant threat to their security. The study also provides a comprehensive analysis of the side-channel attack surface in IMPs, including a detailed examination of the Myx16 architecture and its security implications. The research demonstrates that side-channel attacks can be used to extract sensitive information from IMPs, including the memory contents and the execution state of the system. The study also identifies key security concerns and provides recommendations for mitigating these risks.

The LHCb experiment at CERN has the potential to measure the polarization of the $\Lambda_b$ baryon, which could provide valuable information about its decay into a $\Lambda_K^0$ and a $J/\psi$. This decay can be analyzed using a specific framework, which involves the reduced polarization kernels. These kernels can be used to calculate the polarization of the $\Lambda_b$ baryon, and they can be expressed in terms of the helicity amplitudes. A new method for calculating the reduced polarization kernels has been developed, which involves a mathematical transformation of the helicity amplitudes. This method can be used to simplify the calculation of the reduced polarization kernels, and it can be applied to other decays as well. The reduced polarization kernels can be used to calculate the polarization of the $\Lambda_b$ baryon, and they can be used to test the consistency of the decay data.

Seismic data often contains significant noise, particularly in shallow areas, which hinders the interpretation of subsurface data. To address this challenge, a novel blind-spot noise reduction method has been developed, leveraging deep learning and transfer education. This approach utilizes a self-supervised convolutional neural network to create a model that can identify noise patterns, and then fine-tunes it to remove noise from seismic data. The method's effectiveness is demonstrated through experiments on synthetic and real-world data, showcasing its ability to eliminate shallow noise while preserving the integrity of deeper subsurface features.

In the context of elastic lepton- and antilepton-proton scattering, we investigate the impact of charge-asymmetric proton form factor terms on scattering observables. Specifically, we examine the effects of photon emissions, which are not accounted for in traditional elastic scattering measurements. By analyzing the effects of these terms on various scattering observables, we find that they can be distinguished from other charge-asymmetric terms, such as those involving the weak interaction. Furthermore, we discuss the potential for these effects to be observed in upcoming experiments at facilities like JLab-12 GeV and EIC.

The compound Sr$_2$IrO$_4$ is a unique material that exhibits a spin-orbit Mott insulating state, characterized by a specific type of magnetic order. In this state, electrons are confined to a particular energy level, resulting in a specific type of excitation that can be described using a particular model. Using advanced scanning tunneling spectroscopy techniques, researchers have been able to measure the energy levels of these excitations and compare them to theoretical predictions. The results show that the energy levels of these excitations are in good agreement with theoretical models, and that the energy levels of these excitations are relatively low compared to the energy required to remove an electron from the material. These findings provide new insights into the behavior of electrons in complex materials and may help to develop new materials with unique properties.

Causal mediation analysis seeks to identify the underlying mechanisms that explain the relationship between a treatment and an outcome. A key method for this analysis is the conditional mediation formula, which enables researchers to quantify the extent to which a treatment's effect on an outcome is mediated by a specific pathway. However, this approach is limited by the need to make assumptions about the relationship between the treatment and the outcome, and between the mediator and the outcome. To address this limitation, we propose a new method called multiply sturdy causal mediation analysis, which allows for the identification of mediation effects under weaker assumptions. Our method is based on the idea that the effect of the treatment on the outcome can be decomposed into a direct effect and an indirect effect, and that the indirect effect can be estimated using a simpler model that does not require strong assumptions. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method using both simulated and real data, and show that it can provide more accurate estimates of mediation effects than traditional methods.

This special edition honors the legacy of the 2018 "Starshades" conference held at the Optical Society's flagship event, "Optics in Space," which took place in August. A comprehensive overview of the conference's significance and its lasting impact on the field is provided, along with a reflection on the conversation surrounding starshades and space-based exoplanet research.

A significant challenge in developing effective suicide prevention systems is the scarcity of annotated data. To address this, Robin, a large-scale, annotated dataset of over 1.2 million tweets containing 10,000 manually labeled tweets, has been created. Robin offers a diverse range of suicidal content, making it distinct from other datasets. To facilitate its use, Robin comes with a pre-trained model that can automatically label tweets, and a tool for managing annotations, making it an invaluable resource for researchers. Robin is now available for public use.

The growing awareness of data privacy has led to the development of numerous technical solutions, but the process of applying these solutions is not always clear. This study examines how data privacy professionals utilize technical solutions, focusing on the practical aspects of implementation. A qualitative research approach was used to investigate the process of implementing technical solutions, including the challenges faced, the role of professionals, and the impact of organizational factors. A total of 30 semi-structured interviews were conducted with data privacy professionals, and the results revealed that professionals often struggle with the practical application of solutions, while organizational factors such as the lack of expertise and the need for collaboration play a significant role. The study highlights the importance of organizational factors in the implementation process and the need for further research to understand the process of implementing technical solutions.

Our research focuses on the simultaneous emission of multiple particles in high-energy proton-nucleus collisions, specifically examining the relationship between particles emitted in different planes. We've analyzed the data in terms of both the number of particles emitted and the distribution of their transverse momentum. We've found that the data aligns with our theoretical model, which takes into account the effects of multiple interactions and the properties of the produced particles. We've also investigated the relationship between the data and the properties of the produced particles, specifically their mass and the size of the collision system. We've found that the data can be used to study the properties of the produced particles and the effects of multiple interactions in high-energy proton-nucleus collisions.

The study of the BEVALAC facility's 4 $\pi$ hadron multiplicity distributions in Au-Au collisions at 1 GeV/nucleon reveals that the formation of light nuclei is a result of diverse coalescence mechanisms. The observed data can be effectively explained by a model that combines a thermal distribution of nucleons with a coalescence mechanism. The model's parameters, including the temperature and the exponent, are determined by fitting the data, and the results show that the formation of light nuclei is a result of both thermal and coalescence processes. The study also found that the formation of light nuclei is a result of the coalescence of nucleons that are in thermal equilibrium with the surrounding medium. The results of the study provide new insights into the formation of light nuclei in heavy-ion collisions and the behavior of the quark-gluon plasma.

The presence of life on Earth heavily relies on the atmosphere and surface liquid water, which are both influenced by a planet's magnetic field and the stability of its surface. As a result, the study of planetary atmospheres and surfaces is a crucial aspect of the search for life beyond our solar system. This article examines the current understanding of rocky exoplanet environments, including the composition of their atmospheres, the occurrence of surface water, and the potential for life. It also explores the challenges and opportunities in the field, as well as the potential for the discovery of life on exoplanets.

The circulant graph, specifically $C_n(i_1, i_2, \dots i_k)$, is a type of undirected graph with $n$ vertices, where $n$ is greater than or equal to the sum of $i_1$ and $i_2$. $C_n(i_1, i_2, \dots i_k)$ is a special case of circulant networks, which are defined by vertices $0, 1, \dots, n-1$ and edges connecting vertices $u$ and $u+i_j$ modulo $n$. In this study, we examine the solvability of certain circulant networks, with a particular focus on the solvability of the following graphs with $n$ vertices: $C_n(1, k)$, $C_n(1, k)$ combined with $C_n(1, k+2)$, and $C_n(1, k)$ combined with $C_n(1, k+3)$.

A novel approach to efficiently compute the inverse of a matrix has been developed,
building upon earlier methods that utilized the augmented matrix technique.
This new method, known as elevated order techniques (EOT), achieves a faster
computation time by leveraging the properties of augmented matrices.
This work extends the existing EOT by incorporating the concept of multiple
augmented matrices, resulting in an enhanced method that converges more rapidly.
This improved method, referred to as the multiple augmented order technique
(MAOT), has been further optimized to take advantage of the capabilities of
graphics processing units (GPUs).

We investigate the influence of back-reaction effects on the primordial power spectrum during ultra-slow-roll inflation, focusing on the period where these effects are most pronounced. Utilizing a stochastic inflation approach, we derive an expression for the primordial power spectrum, accounting for the effects of incoherent quantum fluctuations. Our analysis reveals that, during ultra-slow-roll inflation, back-reaction effects significantly impact the power spectrum, causing a notable decrease in its value. Furthermore, we demonstrate that, in the ultra-slow-roll regime, the power spectrum is directly proportional to the third-order cumulant of the inflaton field, which is generated by quantum fluctuations. Our findings suggest that, in the ultra-slow-roll regime, the primordial power spectrum is significantly lower than in the slow-roll regime, even when quantum fluctuations are considered.

The traditional selection optimization problem involves identifying the optimal subset of $k$ items from a larger set of $n$ items, where each subset is evaluated using a real-valued function. This paper introduces the enhanced selection optimization problem, which expands upon the original problem by allowing for a subset of $k$ items to be chosen from a predefined list of candidate subsets, each containing $k$ items. This new problem is addressed through the application of a novel algorithm, which is shown to be efficient and capable of handling large datasets. The proposed algorithm is then applied to a specific problem, the k-means clustering algorithm, which is a fundamental tool in data analysis and machine learning.

This article presents a novel approach to survival analysis, utilizing a database of cases to facilitate the examination and comparison of event frequencies. The method offers a flexible framework for survival analysis, allowing for the exploration of multiple covariates and their effects on survival outcomes. The approach is demonstrated through a case study of a dataset from the UK's National Cancer Registration and Analysis System, where the impact of cancer type on survival is investigated.

The accuracy of scientific research is significantly influenced by theoretical precision, which in turn relies on precise calculations of complex mathematical integrals. This article reviews the current state of research on a specific class of multi-dimensional integrals and highlights their importance in achieving high levels of precision in scientific studies.

The 3D printing revolution has been driven by the rapid growth of 3D model data, which has become a key component of the manufacturing process. 3D models, which are typically large in size and numerous in quantity, are often stored in a file-based format, but this can be inefficient for processing. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed using object storage, which is designed to handle large numbers of small files. This study compares two object storage options: a new file system called DAOS and a traditional file system called Lustre. The results show that DAOS outperforms Lustre in the object data management approach, making it a more suitable choice for handling 3D model data.

The increasing number of electric vehicles poses a significant challenge to existing traffic management systems, particularly in terms of admission control.  A proposed solution is a digital admission regulation system that can efficiently manage the flow of electric vehicles into public parking facilities.  This system utilizes a digital ticketing system to regulate the admission of electric vehicles, thereby reducing the strain on parking facilities and improving overall traffic management.  A case study was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of this system, and the results showed that it can significantly reduce the time it takes to admit electric vehicles into public parking facilities, thereby reducing traffic congestion and improving overall traffic management.  Moreover, the system can also provide valuable data on the flow of electric vehicles, which can be used to inform future traffic management decisions.  Overall, the results of this study demonstrate that the digital admission regulation system is a viable solution for managing the flow of electric vehicles into public parking facilities, and can help to mitigate the negative impact of the increasing number of electric vehicles on existing traffic management systems.

Low-weight codewords in linear codes can be used to assess their error-correcting capabilities, and a code's LCD property is also influenced by these codewords. This study examines the existence of low-weight codewords in linear codes over finite fields, and investigates how the number of such codewords changes with different field sizes. Additionally, we explore the development of LCD codes from non-LCD codes and derive upper bounds on the number of LCD codes with specific parameters.

We investigate the effects of loop contributions on the Newton potential, particularly when the graviton's kinetic term is suppressed. Our analysis reveals that the one-loop correction to this potential is logarithmic, and we examine the implications of this finding on the Newton potential's behavior at various distance scales. Furthermore, we explore the effects of a large number of matter fields on the Newton potential, and we demonstrate that the correction to this potential is significantly enhanced in the presence of such matter fields. We also investigate the effects of a large number of matter fields on the Newton potential's behavior at various distance scales, and we examine the implications of these findings for the validity of general relativity.

The transition to a low-carbon economy relies heavily on the adoption of renewable energy sources, but this shift comes with significant implications for land use. Our research examines the trade-offs between land use and cost reduction in the power sector, focusing on the American West. We developed a model that simulates the power grid's operation and incorporates various renewable energy sources, such as solar, wind, and hydropower, as well as existing infrastructure. By analyzing different scenarios, we found that the American West's power sector can achieve a balance between land use and cost reduction, with a notable finding that hydropower is a more efficient option for reducing land use compared to other renewable sources. Our results suggest that the power sector can achieve significant cost reductions without compromising land use efficiency.

In randomized trials with randomly assigned groups, the impact of an intervention is often evaluated through the lens of per-protocol and as-treated analyses, which consider the actual treatment received by participants. However, in studies involving cluster-randomized trials with multiple interventions, the interpretation of these analyses can be complicated by the presence of multiple treatment options. To address this complexity, this study proposes a framework for defining and drawing conclusions from per-protocol and as-treated analyses in such trials. The proposed framework is applied to a cluster-randomized trial examining the effectiveness of the pneumococcal conjugate vaccine in children in Kenya, where the study also investigates the effects of the intervention on pneumococcal disease in the surrounding community.

This study focuses on the fractal M\"obius octagonal network, a class of graphs generated through an iterative process. We derive the analytical form of the Laplacian matrix for these networks and calculate its eigenvalues. We also introduce the concept of the standardized Laplacian matrix and derive its analytical eigenvalues. We then apply the calculated spectral properties to determine the network's connectivity and identify its most and least significant nodes.

In the field of machine learning, a significant area of research is contextual linear bandits, which involves a learner receiving context information and selecting actions from a predefined set to maximize rewards. The learner's objective is to minimize the cumulative regret by making informed decisions. A key challenge in this area is when the context information is held by multiple agents, each with its own unique perspective. In this scenario, a central coordinator is tasked with aggregating the context information and making a decision on behalf of the agents. A novel algorithm has been developed to address this issue, which achieves optimal regret bounds in both stochastic and adversarial settings. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated through simulations, showcasing its ability to outperform existing methods in a variety of scenarios.

Cancer and cystic fibrosis are among the leading causes of mortality in the United States. Research has shown that the use of predictive models in healthcare can significantly improve patient care and outcomes. However, the development of such models is hindered by the lack of high-quality, relevant data. To address this issue, we have developed a synthetic dataset of cystic fibrosis patients, which can be used to train predictive models and advance healthcare research. This dataset, which includes clinical and demographic information, was created using a combination of statistical and machine learning techniques. The resulting data is indistinguishable from real-world data, making it a valuable resource for researchers and healthcare professionals.

A thorough examination of the $D^0$ decay into $K^\mp \pi^\pm \pi^\pi^\mp$ has been conducted, with a focus on the $K\pi$ invariant mass spectrum. The investigation utilized a substantial dataset of $1.0$ fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb detector, resulting in a significant discovery of the $D^0$ decaying into $K^\mp \pi^\mp \pi^+$ and $K^\mp \pi^+$, with a statistical significance of $10.2$ standard deviations. The analysis also identified the presence of a new $f_0$ state, with a mass of $1.44$ GeV/c$^2$ and a width of $100$ MeV/c$^2$, as well as a previously known $f_0(980)$ state, with a mass of $980$ MeV/c$^2$ and a width of $70$ MeV/c$^2$. The investigation also provided a precise measurement of the branching fraction of the $D^0$ decaying into $K^\mp \pi^\mp \pi^+$, with a value of $(1.11 \pm 0.09 \pm 0.10)$, with the first error being statistical and the second being systematic.

This paper presents a software tool called Novelpy, a Python library for bibliometric analysis, that quantifies the originality and distinctiveness of scientific publications and inventions. The library's functionality is grounded in a mathematical framework that measures the average proximity of a document's cited references within a bibliographic network. This framework is then translated into practical Python code, leveraging Network1D, a Python package for efficient bibliographic network analysis. The paper showcases the library's capabilities through a series of experiments using real-world data from the USPTO, and provides guidance on its installation and usage.

We have developed a method to control the intensity of an optical pulse by leveraging cross-phase modulation with a reference pulse. This technique enables the precise manipulation of the reference pulse's temporal and spatial characteristics, and we demonstrate its application in generating complex spatiotemporal laser beams.

The primary objective of this research is to investigate the feasibility of using a machine to shoot a recurve bow, which is a relatively underexplored area of study. Our analysis delves into the existing literature on machines shooting bows, which is limited, and examines the existing knowledge on recurve bows, which is more extensive. Our findings indicate that a machine can indeed shoot a recurve bow, but it may not be able to match the accuracy of a skilled human archer. Our future work will focus on building a prototype to test this hypothesis and conduct experiments to compare the accuracy of the machine to that of a human.

A major challenge in cross-domain recommendation is that users' preferences in the target domain are often underrepresented in the target domain interaction matrix. To address this issue, we propose a novel method that leverages the target domain's implicit feedback to develop a more efficient approach. Our method utilizes the target domain's implicit feedback to create a novel loss function that incorporates dual metrics, allowing for more accurate recommendations. By training the model with this dual loss function, we can effectively capture users' preferences in the target domain and improve the accuracy of the recommendations. Our method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of both accuracy and efficiency, and we also demonstrate that it can be easily integrated into existing models.

The thermal transfer between a hot, confined plasma and its cooler surroundings is a critical component of fusion reactor design. We've developed a computational model to simulate the thermal transfer in intricate plasma layers, taking into account the complex geometry of these systems. Our model, based on a 2D simulation, incorporates the effects of plasma diffusion and radiation, and can be applied to various scenarios, including those with varying levels of complexity. We've tested the model using a simplified scenario, and the results show good agreement with analytical solutions. Our model can be used to study the thermal transfer in more complex systems, and can be adapted to include additional effects, such as plasma convection.

We examine a statistical model that combines multiple unordered collections of data, each comprised of $d$-dimensional vectors. The data sets are weighted by non-negative coefficients that sum to one, and their distribution is represented as a weighted sum of individual multivariate normal distributions. We investigate the model's properties, including its identifiability and the behavior of its maximum likelihood estimators, and we also consider a least squares estimation method for this class of mixtures.

In cardio-angiography, fluoroscopy is a crucial imaging technique, but it exposes patients to potentially hazardous X-ray radiation. To mitigate this risk, we've developed a deep learning-based method to reduce the radiation dose during the procedure. Our approach involves using fluoroscopy images captured at low X-ray doses to train a deep neural network, which can then enhance images captured at even lower doses. By comparing our method to traditional image denoising techniques, we've found that it significantly improves image quality, as measured by the peak signal-to-noise ratio. Moreover, our method allows for a substantial reduction in X-ray exposure, up to 90%, without compromising image quality.

The future electron-positron collider, FCC-ee, will offer groundbreaking opportunities for the study of heavy flavors, particularly charm and bottom quarks, due to its unparalleled ability to produce large quantities of these particles at the Z peak. This unique capability will enable researchers to conduct precise measurements of GIM-suppressed mixing elements and rare decays, as well as investigations into the GIM mechanism and CKM unitarity. This article discusses the scientific potential of FCC-ee, its prospects for precision measurements, and the technological challenges that must be addressed to achieve these goals.

A black hole at the center of a binary system with a massive star can cause the ejection of stars, including those with significant velocities, through the process of mass exchange and gravitational interactions. This process, which involves the secular perturbation of the binary by the black hole, can result in the ejection of stars, including those with velocities exceeding the escape velocity of the galaxy. This ejection mechanism is particularly effective in binary systems with a mass ratio of approximately 1, and can result in the ejection of stars with velocities up to 1000 km/s. This ejection mechanism is predicted to be the dominant source of hypervelocity stars in the galaxy, and can also explain the presence of stars with high velocities in the galaxy.

We investigate a given stochastic differential equation, which is a modified form of the Kolmogorov equation, with a stochastic perturbation that is influenced by a Brownian motion. Under specific conditions, we show that this equation has a unique solution, which is a continuous path, even when it is subjected to large stochastic disturbances.
